result:
There's a particular pleasure in words that sound like what they mean, and a different, almost opposite pleasure in words that betray their meaning entirely. "Susurrus" hisses appropriately, all those soft consonants rustling like the leaves it's used to describe. But "gregarious" sounds nothing like a person who enjoys company—it sounds clinical, vaguely medical, like something you'd find in a diagnosis. I think about this more than is probably useful: the strange non-relationship between sound and sense, how a word like "moist" can repulse people not because of any inherent ugliness in its phonemes but because of cultural accretion, a kind of collective flinch that's been trained into a population through repetition and mockery until the word itself seems to curdle.

Languages are full of these little betrayals and accidents. "Nice" used to mean foolish, then ignorant, then precise, then pleasant—a word that wandered through almost contradictory meanings over centuries like someone slowly forgetting who they used to be. There's something comforting in that history, actually. It suggests meaning isn't fixed, that language is less like a building and more like a river, the same name attached to different water flowing past at different times.

I keep coming back to the idea of attention as a kind of currency, maybe because it's so often described that way now—"the attention economy," as if our gaze were a coin and the internet a marketplace designed to extract it from our pockets. But attention isn't quite like money. You can't save it. You can't really borrow against it. It exists only in the spending, and the moment you try to hoard it—to multitask, to split it across six tabs and a podcast and a half-eaten sandwich—it degrades, like a photocopy of a photocopy. There's an irony in writing about attention while assuming someone is reading this with divided focus, maybe scrolling toward something else already. I don't resent that. It's just the texture of how people read now, in fragments, in the in-between moments of a day that rarely offers an in-between.

Sometimes I think about the difference between noticing and looking. You can look at a tree for an hour and not notice anything in particular—the eye simply registers green, brown, vertical, familiar, and moves on, satisfied that it has filed the experience correctly. Noticing requires friction. It requires the tree to surprise you somehow: a branch growing at an angle that seems almost rebellious, a knot in the bark that resembles a closed eye, the particular way afternoon light makes the leaves translucent at the edges, like stained glass that's been left out in the rain too long. Noticing is slower than looking, and less efficient, and probably this is why it's becoming rarer—not because people have changed fundamentally but because the architecture of daily life rewards the fast scan over the slow look. Everything is designed to be glanced at and judged in under a second: an app icon, a headline, a stranger's profile picture. Noticing doesn't fit into that economy. It's almost an act of resistance, mundane and private, the kind of thing nobody will ever know you did except you.

I wonder about animals and whether they notice things the way we imagine we do, or whether their attention is purer, less narrated. A dog smelling a fire hydrant for four straight minutes seems, from the outside, like a study in pure noticing—total absorption, no internal monologue commenting on the absorption, no part of the dog's mind drafting a sentence about how interesting this fire hydrant is. Maybe that's the difference: human noticing is always slightly haunted by its own narration. Even as I write this, I'm aware that I'm writing about noticing rather than simply noticing, which is its own kind of remove, like trying to describe the taste of water while drinking it.

There's a particular kind of silence that exists only briefly, in the seconds after a loud noise stops—a kind of after-silence that's louder, somehow, than ordinary quiet, because it's defined by what it's the absence of. I don't know if there's a word for this in any language, though there probably should be. German seems like the kind of language that would have a word for it, something long and specific and slightly absurd to an English speaker, the way "Kummerspeck"—grief bacon, the weight gained from emotional eating—manages to be both poetic and faintly ridiculous at once.

I think a lot about ridiculousness as an underrated quality. Most things that matter are at least a little ridiculous if you look at them straight on. Love is ridiculous—the way it makes people text things like "thinking of u :)" with genuine sincerity, the way it survives despite every reasonable argument against its continuation. Ambition is ridiculous, all those plans laid against the certainty of death, as if building something that lasts matters when nothing ultimately does, and yet we build anyway, write anyway, plant trees we won't live to see grow tall. Grief is ridiculous too, in its way—the disproportion of it, how a person who took up maybe five feet ten inches of physical space can leave a hole that swallows whole years.

Maybe what I'm circling, without quite landing on it, is that meaning doesn't require justification to be real. The susurrus of leaves doesn't need to mean anything to be worth noticing. The dog at the fire hydrant isn't performing a metaphor for presence; it's just a dog, doing what dogs do, untroubled by whether its absorption is profound. Perhaps the trick—if there is one—is to notice more and narrate less, to let the tree be strange without immediately turning that strangeness into a sentence. Though clearly, today, I haven't quite managed that.
